data.title: Trump admin ends $45M support for Namibia HIV program
data.description:
The Trump administration announced it will be ending $45 million in support for Namibia’s HIV response program following two decades of annual payments.

The U.S. will provide its final $45 million payment in the 2027 fiscal year as “this support will transition into a technical cooperation model,” according to a Friday joint statement from Namibia’s Ministry of International Relations & Trade and the U.S. Embassy in Namibia.

“This transition is a celebration of Namibia’s leadership and a model for what is possible,” U.S. Ambassador to Namibia John Giordano said in the statement.

Namibia will now integrate its HIV response into a “sustainable national health system” that is “guided by Namibia’s priorities, policies and legal frameworks.” 

The U.S.-backed program previously supported “investments in HIV testing, counselling, community-based organizations and other key health system intervention.”

The joint U.S.-Namibian effort notably surpassed global targets for HIV testing, treatment and viral suppression during its tenure, reporting that 97 percent of infants born to HIV-positive mothers tested negative for the disease. 

“As we evolve this partnership, we remain committed to a cooperation model that respects Namibia’s sovereignty and the integrity of our national health data,” said Dr. Esperance Luvindao, the Namibian Health minister.

The decision follows Namibia’s rejection of provisions that would have required the country to share sensitive health data with the U.S.,

According to The Namibian, the end of funding follows Namibia rejecting U.S. efforts to require the country to share sensitive health data as part of continued U.S. support.

Officials told the outlet that, “the Namibian government has made it unequivocally clear that the data-sharing or specimen-sharing agreements in their proposed forms are not in compliance with Namibia’s national laws.”

A report by the Kaiser Family Foundation and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) found that global HIV response plunged in 2025 blaming a steep decline in U.S. support. 

The Trump administration previously created the “America First Global Health Strategy” that called for significant scale-down in U.S. funding for countries in the future, including global health programs which it called “inefficient and wasteful and created a culture of dependency among recipient countries.”

Other changes made by the administration include freezing and ultimately canceling global HIV projects, eliminating the U.S. Agency for International Development and canceling support to UNAIDS in 2025.

data.title: Trump's MAGA Inc. super-PAC funnels $10 million into Ken Paxton's Senate campaign
data.description:
President Trump’s super-PAC MAGA Inc. gave $10 million to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published Saturday.

The $10 million payment, given to political media company, Del Ray Media, funded two attack ads against his Democratic opponent James Talarico — who is running a surprisingly competitive race in the historically red Lone Star State. 

A MAGA Inc. spokesperson, Alex Pfeiffer, told The Hill the MAGA Inc.-funded ads focus on how “High Tax Talarico” is planning to “take money out of Texans’ pockets.”

“MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico’s radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate,” Pfeiffer said in her Saturday statement.

Talarico has made promises to put a higher tax on billionaires while cutting taxes for working families and small businesses, while Paxton has advocated for tax breaks and tackling the ongoing affordability crisis. 

The Lone Star Liberty PAC is slated to run similar attack ads against Talarico in September for being sympathetic to China, as the current state representative voted against legislation last year establishing criminal penalties for foreign entities purchasing Texas land.

The spending comes after Republican strategist Karl Rove said Wednesday that the “time is running out” for Paxton, who some polls have placed behind his opponent.

 “Of the president wants to have Paxton win, he needs to be tossing a lot of money Paxton’s way so that ads can be run that depict Talarico as the far-left winger that he is,” Rove said.

Trump said yesterday the PAC has $1 billion at its disposal amid Republicans’ calls for him to invest further in midterm candidates, though reports from June estimated its finances at around $400 million. He added that MAGA Inc. plans to spend between $400 and $500 million for November’s midterms, saving the rest for the 2028 election cycle.

Paxton pulled ahead in the Republican primary when he earned the president’s endorsement, though he has struggled to build a sustainable lead over his opponent since the primaries

Despite Trump winning the Lone Star state by around 14 points in the 2024 presidential election, Paxton trailed Talarico by 6-points in an August poll from Texas Public Opinion Research. 

The Republican has also faced several notable scandals, including the Texas state House voting to impeach him on corruption charges — of which the state senate later acquitted him.

Democrats are increasingly hopeful they can flip Texas’ seat, which Republicans have held for the last three decades. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report also shifted the Texas Senate race to a toss-up — citing Paxton’s high disapproval ratings and “notably underperforming even a generic Republican in GOP polling.”

data.title: Trump faces down beef backlash. Will import plan pay off?
data.description:
President Trump is pushing ahead with his plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans, despite the backlash from cattle farmers and Republicans whose states would be most be most affected.

In an apparent effort to soften the blow, Trump signed executive orders Friday, including one that allows ranchers and farmers to process and package their own products, and another that promotes country-of-origin labeling across all foreign beef, which would require congressional action.

Justin Tupper, president of the United States Cattlemen’s Association, said it appreciated the new orders but remained “cautious on what comes next.”

Following the signings in the Oval Office, Trump sought to play down the impact of his beef import plan, telling reporters, “We’re doing it in a very limited fashion because our ranchers can handle it,” adding, “Our ranchers want the prices to be down too.” 

When announcing the move last month to import 300,000 metric tons of beef without tariffs for 90 days, Trump said the beef would be sold at 25 percent below current market prices. He revealed for the first time Friday the beef would be coming primarily from Brazil and Argentina.

Those critical of the move say it will barely move the needle on Americans’ cost-of-living concerns, while forcing a key part of Trump’s base to pay a heavy price. 

“Trump is right to address the issue of beef prices but stepped in it in doing so in a way that parts of his base are going to react to,” said Doug Heye, a longtime GOP strategist. 

“The administration — and Trump in particular — need to be spending all their efforts on lowering prices across the board, including the latest cost driver, Iran,” he added.

Glynn Tonsor, an assistant professor in the Kansas State University Department of Agricultural Economics, said the odds of this deal lowering prices and helping ranchers “are about zero.”

“If there’s something that reduces beef prices for consumers, by definition, that reduces the dollars going back into the industry, because the price clearing the market for retail beef is lower, and therefore one has to pause and say, is that good for producers?” he said. “So, there’s a world where one or the other might happen, but I don’t see any world where both could happen out of the same announcement.”

The 300,000 metric ton figure only represents about a 2 percent increase in beef supply, Tonsor noted. 

“I’m on record saying it’ll have very, very small, if any, impact on the price that consumers pay for beef,” he said.

Beef prices have been soaring across the country. The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound in the U.S. is roughly $6.89, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

The prices have gone up because the U.S. is raising record-low cattle numbers due to several factors, including droughts and rising operational costs, all the while demand remains high.

Data from the Department of Agriculture showed that the U.S started with 86.2 million cattle at the beginning of the year, the lowest cattle inventory since 1951.

Affordability, meanwhile, remains a top issue for voters ahead of the midterms. Trump captured 62 percent of the rural vote in 2024, but his approval among that voter group has fallen from July to August, according to polls done by ActiVote.

The cattle industry and GOP lawmakers argue that lowering prices for Americans shouldn’t come at the cost of America’s ranchers.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,” Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement. 

“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” he added, saying the import plan throws “cold water” on the investment necessary to expand herds.

David Anderson, a professor and extension specialist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University, said the markets should have been left to work themselves out.

“You have to have cattle producers that are profitable to get that market signal to expand, to increase beef production which then brings down prices,” Anderson said. “And so, we finally have prices that are profitable and something like this gets announced.”

He said it comes at a bad time when ranchers are making decisions about their herds.

“This was just another announcement, another thing hitting the market to drive down prices,” he said. “Lowering prices reduces that incentive to expand.”

Several Republican lawmakers have spoken out too. Sens. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and Jerry Moran (Kan.), Rep. Adrian Smith (Neb.) and 50 others wrote a letter to Trump urging him to prioritize policies that would help ranchers.

“Cattle markets are cyclical, and ranchers use the upswings to prepare for the inevitable downturn,” the lawmakers wrote. “Any intervention in the natural system, especially at a time when producers are making marketing decisions, threatens to pick winners and losers and undermine the long-term viability of family-owned cattle operations throughout the supply chain.” 

A report from The Wall Street Journal earlier this past week said that Trump met with Joesley Batista, who shares control of JBS, the world’s largest meatpacker, in the Oval Office a day before he made the announcement. 

The sources said that during the meeting, Batista lobbied Trump to drop the import tax as a way to mitigate costs of beef for consumers.

In response to the report, the White House said Trump’s “action to address a short-term supply crunch in the beef market was the result of a long policy planning and coordination process involving domestic stakeholders; this action was not done as the result of any one conversation.”

Brandon Scholz, a former Republican turned independent political analyst from Wisconsin, said Trump’s move gives a “false sense of hope to consumers … and then we’re going to start losing our producers and our growers.”

“I think he’s just putting out a false sense of security in front of the midterms,” Scholz said. “I simply can’t imagine that this is something that people are going to go to the voting booth and go, ‘You know, that was really great that Trump got us all that cheap beef.’”

data.title: Trump shakes up RNC midterm convention schedule, says he'll speak on night one
data.description:
President Trump is set to speak on Night 1 of the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9.

“The Greatest RALLY of them all,” Trump wrote in a Friday Truth Social post. “I’ll be speaking on night one, and hanging around for an earlier closing, and lots of music, on night two!!! See you in Dallas.”

Vice President J.D. Vance was originally scheduled to deliver the keynote address for night one, with President Trump capping off night two. It’s unclear how the president’s announcement will affect the previously announced schedule.

Trump had previously hinted in an August statement that he would “be with you both nights.”

The first-of-its-kind convention is expected to have Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate in the Lone Star State, in attendance. 

Other Republican politicians stated they could not attend – including Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) saying he could no longer attend as campaign events were added to his schedule and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) instead meeting with constituents that weekend, according to Newsweek.

The convention shakeup comes as a GOP operative tells the Hill that while Trump has been touting the event for a year, because it was only announced in late June, candidates and incumbents have not been given nearly as much time to plan their participation.

“Lot of things made this very hasty that didn’t need to happen,” the operative said.

Some House members are opting to not attend the convention due to a reported $25,000 in minimum expected contributions, with the highest tier asking for $100,000.

The programming for the event lists over 100 items the RNC will cover such as “Education & Parental Rights” and a panel of Republican candidates campaigning in swing districts across the country.

The RNC will also be “honoring Charlie Kirk’s impact on American youth and converting that legacy into a call to mobilize voters,” on the same day that the political commentator was killed a year ago.

data.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump travels to Texas for RNC midterm convention; Administration downplays Iran war consequences
data.description:
President Trump will head to the GOP’s convention in Dallas next week — an event aimed at galvanizing Republican voters to get out the vote ahead of the midterm elections this November. 

The president will headline the two-day convention, and Vice President JD Vance is also expected to address attendees.

Ahead of the inaugural event, Trump-affiliated super PAC MAGA Inc. gave $10 million to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) campaign — placating some Republicans calls for the president to invest in GOP candidates locked in toss-up races with Democratic challengers.

Trump said yesterday the PAC has $1 billion at its disposal, though reports from June estimated its finances at around $400 million. The president said yesterday MAGA Inc. plans to spend between $400 and $500 million for November’s midterms, saving the rest for the 2028 election cycle.

The convention comes amid rising frustration among voters with the president’s handling of the economy and the Iran war. 

The Trump administration has attempted to calm concerns about the monthslong conflict, with Vice President Vance telling reporters this week he “wouldn’t call it a war.”

House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) will join CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday, likely set to discuss how Republicans are approaching the November elections.

In a bid to bring down rising U.S. fuel costs tied to global energy shortages during the Iran war, last week the president announced a new deal with Venezuela to gain “majority U.S. control” of a large portion of the country’s massive oil reserves. 

Trump’s economic approval rating has taken a hit, as gas prices have hit record highs. This new agreement gives the U.S. a 55 percent “effective output” in 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven reserves, but experts told The Hill it could be a while before this move impacts U.S. gas prices. 

Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who has championed this new deal, will appear on several Sunday shows, including “Face the Nation,” CNN’s “State of the Union,” Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday” and ABC News’s “This Week.”

Additionally, the president signed several executive orders this week aimed at bringing down beef costs for American consumers, including a controversial directive to lower high tariffs on imported beef products from countries like Brazil and Argentina. 

Ranchers, farmers and some Republican lawmakers have balked at the move, saying it would negatively impact the sale of domestic beef, since these imported goods would be sold at 25 percent under market price. 

The U.S. will pause “out-of-quota” tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of beef for a 90–day period in an effort to bring down costs and allow the U.S. cattle population to regrow. 

The president sought to address these concerns by adding a new requirement for foreign beef to be labeled with its country-of-origin and allowing American ranchers to process their own meat. The Friday order also asked the Interior Department to consider stripping the grey wolf, a livestock predator, of its endangered species protections. 

A day later, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in an attempt to reopen peace negotiations and end its yearslong war with Ukraine. The pair will then travel to Kyiv to talk with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday. 

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), a senior member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, will join Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures” this weekend.. 

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s announced resignation on Monday marked the latest departure from the Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth, who has faced mounting scrutiny for his attempts to impose his will on the service branch, is reportedly considering Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell to replace Driscoll, sources told The Hill. 

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), a member of the House Committee on Armed Services, called this week for Trump to fire Hegseth. The Democrat will join The Hill’s “The Hill Sunday” this weekend. 

The Pentagon’s leadership has also come under fire for its attempts to reshape the Stars and Stripes. 

Three of the military outlet’s staffers sued the department last week after they were fired amid Pentagon leadership’s effort to crack down on “woke” coverage. On Friday, a federal judge on Friday denied their request to stop these terminations. 

Former Stars and Stripes publisher, Max Lederer, told MS NOW on Saturday morning that he and the two other fired staffers will continue their lawsuit against the department, noting the emergency injunction was only the “first step in the process.”

In another legal battle, Missouri asked the Supreme Court late Friday to restore a congressional map that favors Republicans after a lower court ruled earlier in the week it could not be used in the midterm elections. 

In Maryland, the state’s highest court ruled in favor of keeping a Democrat-drawn redistricting referendum on the ballot. If approved, this measure would grant the state’s General Assembly the authority to give the Maryland Supreme Court “original jurisdiction” over congressional redistricting plans, which would likely make it easier for Democrats to win seats.

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin (D) will join NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday.  

See the full list of guests on the Sunday morning news shows below:

NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday”: Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas)

CBS News’s “Face the Nation”: Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D), House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.)

CNN’s “State of the Union”: Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D)

Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday”: Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Andy McCarthy

NBC News’s “Meet the Press”: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.)

Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures”: Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), Minnesota U.S. Senate candidate Michele Tafoya (R), Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas)

ABC’s “This Week”: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox (R), Energy Secretary Chris Wright, former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III

data.title: Texas Republican: 'I don't have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy'
data.description:
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children.

“I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy,” Gill said Friday on Fox News’s “The Will Cain Show.”

“I have an enormous amount of sympathy for the three little innocent kids who were slaughtered,” he said earlier.

Gill went on to push back against the central argument of Clancy’s defense: that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at the family’s Massachusetts home in 2023.

“You don’t get licensed to murder your children or anybody else just because you have mental health problems,” Gill said. “We’ve gotten in a habit of medicalizing evil.”

Trial Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when jurors remained deadlocked for seven days without being able to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

A last-minute attempt was made by Clancy’s attorneys to remove the lone holdout juror, whom they accused of refusing to properly apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to remove the juror.

The legal battle has dominated national headlines, with even President Trump weighing in to respond to news of the mistrial.

“It’s a shame. It’s a horrible tragedy,” Trump said when asked about the case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. “She did a horrible, horrible thing.”

“I guess they’re going to go through another trial. It’s too bad,” he concluded.

data.title: Huckabee calls Israeli settler violence in West Bank an 'act of terror'
data.description:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Wednesday called Israeli settler violence in the West Bank an “act of terror,” condemning their actions.

Huckabee said his visit was for the U.S. citizens “who live in Turmusayya and other communities across this region” who are “disturbed by people who have created extraordinary challenges that are unfair and illegal.”

While acknowledging that he’s been “criticized a little bit for calling that terror,” he defended his statements as fitting the definition of terrorism in remarks at Turmusayya Town Hall, labeling these settlers as a “band of terrorists” engaged in “criminal activity.”

“It’s important that we continue to put the pressure to say letting a few people do these horrible activities of criminal nature is detrimental…to everyone, Israeli, Palestinian alike,” he said.

This isn’t the first time Huckabee has violent Israeli settlers as “terrorists.” In August, he condemned settlers for besieging a Palestinian village and the home of a Palestinian American in the West Bank town of Qusra. 

Huckabee said that the settlers burned a mosque and graffitied, “Huckabee, this is from the terrorist” on a wall in the village.

Huckabee’s continued remarks are an unusually strong response from the Trump administration related to Israeli settlers as President Trump previously dropped sanctions against violent Israeli settlers imposed by the Biden administration.

“I’m glad they admitted it,” Huckabee said Saturday about the message’s labeling. “I don’t think that’s what they intended to do, but I do think that they represent a very tiny minority.”

The State Department similarly condemned the violence, with a spokesperson saying last week that the department remains in line with the Trump administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region.

data.title: Former Stars and Stripes publisher: Pentagon lawsuit will 'continue on' after court setback
data.description:
Max Lederer, the former longtime publisher of the Stars and Stripes, on Saturday said he and the two other staffers fired by the Pentagon last month will “continue on” in their lawsuit after a federal judge denied their emergency request this week. 

Lederer and the paper’s former editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte sued the Pentagon last week, alleging the department’s decision to dismiss them from their roles violated its own personnel rules and their First Amendment rights. 

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden ruled Friday that the employees were not likely to succeed in their claim that these terminations violated their First Amendment rights. 

Lederer told MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff on Saturday morning that this request was only the “first step in the process,” noting that “it’s a really high bar in a preliminary injunction” and that McFadden’s ruling  “doesn’t eliminate our basic suit.”

“We are going on with that suit,” he said. “That will continue on, and we’ll have more opportunity to present our case to the judge and argue this very important issue.”

The Pentagon’s leadership under President Trump’s second presidency has attempted to reshape the military outlet’s coverage. Chief Pentagon Spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January that the department would “refocus” the organization’s coverage from “woke distractions that syphon morale.”

While the paper is staffed by members of the Defense Department, the Stars and Stripes has historically enjoyed editorial independence from the Pentagon. 

In March, the Pentagon issued an eight-page memo that included a requirement for the paper’s content to be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.”

Two of the organization’s advisory board members sued the department in June, alleging the Pentagon was attempting to “exert unprecedented control” over the paper and sensor its content.

The department also removed the outlet’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, whose job was to monitor the newspaper’s editorial independence. Smith sued the Pentagon in June over this decision.

Prior to his firing, Lederer had announced his retirement and planned to step down from his role overseeing the paper at the end of this month. He told MS NOW on Saturday that he made this decision after declining Pentagon officials’ request to fire two outlet staffers. 

“I had gotten to a point where I couldn’t support the direction any longer, and as any good employee of any good organization, your option is to do what you’re asked to do or leave,” Lederer said. “And I chose to leave.”

data.title: Bettors are harassing college athletes. It's time for Congress to act.
data.description:
Growing up, mom always said, “if you don’t have anything nice to say, then don’t say anything at all.” While she was unaware at the time, this phrase may become pointed legal advice — especially if you are a college sports fan or bettor.

College athletes across the country deal with abusive and vulgar messages from sports fans daily. Take Florida State forward Cam Corhen for example, who after being injured early in a basketball game and only scoring two points, returned to his phone filled with hateful messages from bettors, including one that said, “I hope your mom dies.” Or, North Carolina forward Armando Bacot, who received over one hundred messages demeaning him for having too few rebounds, just 12 days after North Carolina legalized player prop bets on collegiate sports.

Collegiate athlete harassment stemming from sports betting is a widespread issue. One in three high-profile athletes receive abusive messages from people with a betting interest. Student-athletes are demanded to strenuously prepare for their competitions multiple times per day, compete at a high level each week, and simultaneously, perform well academically. Beyond that, in the age of NIL, they are incentivized for maintaining extremely public-facing profiles online. These athletes face an impossible choice: build the public profile NIL demands or protect themselves from relentless online abuse.

Because these young athletes should not have to make such a decision at this stage in their lives, federal legislation is necessary to combat the issue. As legalized sports betting intensifies fan motivation to abusively target athletes, Congress must intervene by implementing a national banned bettors registry for individuals convicted of sports-related harassment and by allowing athletes to sue people who engage in repeated betting related harassment.

Now, it is easier than ever to place bets on individual players via prop bets that allow bettors to place wagers on specific player statistics. This gives fans greater cause to direct their harassment toward individual athletes. Some advocates even argue in favor of banning prop bets on college athletics or eliminating college sports betting altogether. However, because those courses of action are guaranteed to be met with fierce opposition advocacy by the gambling lobby and will take much longer to implement, federal legislation is a better, more expedient option.

This issue has not gone unnoticed, but the measures in place to deter or cure online abuse are failing. Social media or culture campaigns like the NCAA’s “Don’t Be a Loser” initiative encourage fans to be mindful of the statistics underlying gambling related harassment of student-athletes, but awareness campaigns lack teeth.

Additionally, the current legal framework underlying this issue is highly decentralized. Some states ban prop bets and others do not. Some implement banned bettor lists, and some prohibit all sports betting. This structure makes it impossible to protect all collegiate athletes across state lines.

To address this gap, Congress should implement a federal standard that targets online harassment tied to sports betting. First, federal legislation should impose criminal penalties for individuals who engage in online conduct that causes substantial emotional distress or fear for safety. A model for this approach can be found in a New York’s Senate Bill under consideration, which defines harassment in a way that captures the type of abusive and threatening messages these athletes routinely receive. The bill goes even further and designates those individuals convicted of harassment and stalking an amateur athlete as a prohibited sports bettor. A federal standard would ensure consistent treatment across jurisdictions.

Additionally, the legislation should allow collegiate athletes to sue individuals who engage in this type of abusive conduct. The ability to recover monetary damages would create a meaningful deterrent. Because much of this behavior is driven by financial frustration tied to lost wagers, attaching a financial penalty to that behavior directly targets the source of the problem.

Critics may attempt to mount free speech objections, but this narrowly tailored proposed solution is not aimed at criticism or negative commentary about athletic performance. The legislation would focus on true threats and targeted, repeated harassment toward a student-athlete. The Supreme Court has long recognized that speech made with the intent to threaten or intimidate is not protected under the First Amendment. Essentially, fans should feel free to criticize athletes, but not to terrorize them.

A federal approach would standardize accountability in ways state-by-state systems cannot. Rather than relying on inconsistent banned bettor lists and varying state regulations, national legislation would create a baseline level of protection for collegiate athletes, regardless of where they compete or where the harassment originates.

College athletes accept pressure when they step onto the field. They should not have to accept abuse when they step off it. Moving forward requires more than awareness; it requires accountability. Most importantly, it requires a commitment to protecting the well-being of the athletes who make college sports possible.

Deymon X. Fleming, Jr. is a J.D. candidate at the University of Georgia School of Law.

data.title: Kennedy Center closes after ceiling piece falls: 'President Trump has been right'
data.description:
A portion of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer collapsed Friday evening as heavy rain swept through the Washington, D.C. area, prompting officials to temporarily close the main building.

No one was injured in the collapse, according to the Kennedy Center, which released photos from the scene showing chunks of the ceiling and dust scattered across the foyer’s red carpet.

The Grand Foyer, a sprawling hallway connecting the Opera House, Concert Hall and Eisenhower Theater, will remain restricted to visitors and nonessential personnel through the week, according to internal communications obtained by ABC News. The rest of the main building is expected to reopen Saturday.

Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi pointed to the collapse as evidence of the need for extensive renovations at the performing arts complex in a statement to ABC.

She said the ceiling failure “stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership.”

The incident comes as the Kennedy Center is at the center of an ongoing legal fight over its Trump-appointed board’s plans for the building.

The board has approved closing the center for roughly two years for a sweeping renovation. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio member of the board, has challenged the closure plan in federal court.

The dispute also involves efforts to recognize President Trump on the building. The board has sought to add language to the facade crediting Trump with the center’s renovation, a move Beatty is also challenging in court.

The Justice Department has argued that extensive work is necessary to address the building’s condition, citing problems with water damage and rusting steel.

The administration threatened to demolish the building if a judge were to block the center’s closure for repairs, and has repeatedly referred to the center as being in a “decrepit” condition in court filings.
